feedback: If the child predicts the big heavy ice will sink, show a big ice cube floating in a bowl: floating depends on being lighter than the SAME amount of water, not on how big or heavy it is.

If the child thinks the visible tip is the whole thing, let the cube float freely (do not push it) and look from the side through the clear cup — most of it sits below the surface. 'Tip of the iceberg' is literally true.
When the cube keeps bobbing up with its body hidden, point out that this is why icebergs float even though they are enormous.
activities.intendedInsight: Ice floats because frozen water is lighter than the same amount of liquid water; size and weight do not decide it, and most of a floating chunk (like an iceberg) is hidden below the surface.
learnerActions: Get a real ice cube or chunk and a clear cup or tub of water ready.
Before placing the ice in the water, PREDICT out loud whether the big, heavy ice will sink or float, and say WHY first.
Place it in the water and OBSERVE: it floats with only a small part sticking up.
Mark the waterline on the clear cup so you can see how much sits BELOW the surface versus the little tip above.
Try to push the ice all the way under and hold it there, then let go and watch it bob back up every time.
Say in your own words: most of the ice is hidden underwater, and it floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water — not because of how big it is.
activities.title: Push the ice under — and watch it bob back

feedback: If the child treats ice or snow as a different substance, melt a little in the hand — it becomes water, the same stuff just frozen solid.
If the child thinks melting destroys the water, point out the puddle is still water; it can be refrozen back into ice.
Reinforce: solid and liquid swap back and forth; nothing is lost.
activities.intendedInsight: Ice and snow are frozen water (solid); melting turns the solid back into liquid water, and freezing turns liquid back into solid — the water itself is not destroyed or changed into a different substance.
learnerActions: Hold a little ice or snow in a warm hand and watch it turn to water.
Talk about how the puddle is the SAME water, just no longer frozen.
Place liquid water somewhere cold (or imagine the freezer) and describe how it would turn back to solid ice.
Match a picture pair or sequence: ice → melting puddle → refrozen ice, saying which is solid and which is liquid each time.
activities.title: Melt it, freeze it — same water

feedback: If the child says snow is like cotton or sand, show magnified snowflake images so the crystal structure is visible.
If unsure snow is water, melt a pinch in the hand to show it turns to water.
activities.intendedInsight: Snow is made of many tiny frozen ice crystals — it is frozen water, not a fluffy material like cotton or sand.
learnerActions: Look closely at real snowflakes, or at magnified snowflake photographs.
Describe the tiny crystal shapes you can see.
Explain that snow is not like white sand or cotton — it is made of countless tiny frozen ice crystals.
Hold a little snow in a warm hand and watch it melt to water, confirming it is frozen water too.
activities.title: What is snow made of?

feedback: The friend is wrong on both counts: the iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of water, and the part poking up is only a small part while most is hidden below.
If the child judges by size/weight, revisit a big ice cube floating in a bowl.
If the child thinks the tip is the whole thing, let a cube float freely in a clear cup (without pushing it) and look from the side at how much is below.
activities.intendedInsight: A huge, heavy iceberg floats because ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water (size is irrelevant), and the visible tip is only a small part — most is hidden underwater.
learnerActions: Look at a picture or cross-section of a huge iceberg floating with a little poking up above the water.
Respond to a friend's claim: 'Something that big and heavy should sink — and what you see poking up is pretty much the whole thing.'
Say whether the friend is right that it should sink, and whether the bit above water is most of the iceberg or just a little — and explain how you know.
Discuss: Why does a giant iceberg float when a small pebble sinks — is it about size? If most of the iceberg is underwater, why might that be dangerous for a ship?
activities.title: The hidden iceberg (diagnostic discussion)
